summary: Specifies how IS-IS carries IPv6 traffic engineering information so routers can compute traffic-engineered routes that use IPv6 addresses. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: IS-IS routers describe their links to each other so that a path can be planned across the network. This RFC adds the fields that let them describe those links using IPv6 addresses instead of IPv4 ones.

questions: what is ipv6 traffic engineering in is-is
what is the ipv6 srlg tlv
what is tlv type 140 in is-is
what is the ipv6 global interface address tlv
what is the ipv6 te router id tlv
subtitle: New IS-IS TLVs that let routers plan traffic-engineered paths using IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: The traffic engineering TLVs that IS-IS uses to describe links and nodes all identify them with IPv4 addresses, so a network that has moved to IPv6 cannot describe its own paths.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an IPv6 TE Router ID TLV, IPv6 interface and neighbor address sub-TLVs, an IPv6 SRLG TLV and an IPv6 Global Interface Address TLV, with rules on which addresses may appear and where each one travels.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from February 2011 that has not been obsoleted or updated. The new information can be added to an existing IPv4 network without migration work, since only the addressing of the paths changes.

facts.label: New sub-TLV types of TLV 22
facts.value: 12 for the IPv6 Interface Address and 13 for the IPv6 Neighbor Address, each 16 octets

facts.label: IPv6 SRLG TLV length
facts.value: 24 octets, plus 4 per SRLG value, plus 16 if the neighbour address is included

facts.label: Prefix that must not be injected
facts.value: A /128 for the router ID or the interface address

today: RFC 6119 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2011, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. The IPv6 traffic engineering information it defines can be added to an existing IPv4 network without migration work, because only the addressing of the paths changes; moving the paths themselves from IPv4 to IPv6 is a GMPLS signalling question that this document leaves aside.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The IS-IS routing protocol is defined in the ISO standard for the Intermediate System to Intermediate System intra-domain routing information exchange protocol. Each router generates a Link State PDU containing information describing the router and the links from the router. The information in the PDU is encoded in a variable length data structure consisting of a Type, a Length and a Value, and such a data structure is referred to as a TLV.

The traffic engineering extensions of RFC 5305 and the GMPLS extensions of RFC 5307 define a number of TLVs and sub-TLVs that allow traffic engineering information to be disseminated by IS-IS. The addressing information passed in those TLVs is IPv4 specific. RFC 5308 describes how IS-IS can be used to carry out Shortest Path First routing for IPv6, by defining IPv6-specific TLVs analogous to those used for IPv4 addressing.

MPLS traffic engineering is very successful, and as the use of IPv6 grows there is a need to support traffic engineering in IPv6 networks. This document defines the TLVs that allow traffic engineering information, including Generalized MPLS traffic engineering information, to be carried in IPv6 IS-IS networks.

The extensions allow the routing of GMPLS Label Switched Paths using IPv6 addressing through an IS-IS network. There are no migration issues introduced by adding this IPv6 traffic engineering information to an existing IPv4 GMPLS network. Migrating Label Switched Paths themselves from IPv4 to IPv6 is an issue for GMPLS signalling and is outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Every IS-IS router advertises a list of its links, and other routers use that list to work out paths. The traffic engineering part of that list names links and routers with IPv4 addresses. This RFC adds matching fields that use IPv6 addresses.

sections.title: Identifying IS-IS Links with IPv6 Addresses
sections.content:
Each IS-IS link has certain properties: bandwidth, shared risk link groups, switching capabilities, and so on. The IS-IS extensions of RFC 5305 and RFC 5307 describe how to associate these traffic engineering parameters with IS-IS links, and those TLVs use IPv4 addresses to identify the link, or the local and remote link identifiers on unnumbered links.

When IPv6 is used, a numbered link may be identified by IPv4 and by or IPv6 interface addresses. The type of identifier used does not affect the properties of the link, which still has the same bandwidth, shared risk link groups and switching capabilities.

An IPv6 address can have global, unique-local or link-local scope. A global IPv6 address is valid within the scope of the Internet. A unique-local IPv6 address is globally unique but is intended for local communication. A link-local IPv6 address is valid only within the scope of a single link and may only be referenced on that link.

Because the IPv6 traffic engineering TLVs present in LSPs are propagated across networks, they must not use link-local addresses. IS-IS does not need to differentiate between global and unique-local addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPv6 address can be valid everywhere, valid only inside one organisation, or valid only on one cable. The ones that travel between routers have to be the first kind, or at least the second, because a link-local address means nothing on the next hop.

sections.title: The Addresses the Existing TLVs Use
sections.content:
The RFC reviews the IP addresses used in the TLVs defined in RFC 5305 and RFC 5307, and gives an overview of the IPv6 equivalents it needs.

The TE Router ID TLV contains a stable IPv4 address that is routable, regardless of the state of each interface. For IPv6 it is useful to have a stable IPv6 address identifying a traffic engineering node, and the IPv6 TE Router ID TLV provides one.

The IPv4 Interface Address sub-TLV of the Extended IS Reachability TLV contains an IPv4 address for the local end of a link.

The IPv4 Neighbor Address sub-TLV of the Extended IS Reachability TLV is used for point-to-point links and contains an IPv4 address for the neighbor's end of a link. A router constructs it using one of the IPv4 addresses received in the IS-IS Hello PDU from the neighbor on the link.

The IPv6 Neighbor Address sub-TLV holds a globally unique IPv6 address for the interface of the peer, which can be either a global or a unique-local address. The IPv6 Interface Address TLV of RFC 5308 only contains link-local addresses when used in the Hello PDU, so a neighbor's address from that TLV cannot be used when constructing the IPv6 Neighbor Address sub-TLV. Instead the RFC defines an additional TLV, the IPv6 Global Interface Address TLV, which is included in Hello PDUs to provide the globally unique IPv6 address that a neighbor router needs in order to construct the IPv6 Neighbor Address sub-TLV.

The SRLG TLV, type 138, defined in RFC 5307 contains the set of shared risk link groups associated with a link. It identifies the link using either local and remote IPv4 addresses or, for point-to-point unnumbered links, link-local and remote identifiers, and it includes a flags field to indicate which type of identifier is used. When only IPv6 is used, IPv4 addresses and link-local identifiers are not available to identify the link, but IPv6 addresses can be used instead. There is no backward-compatible way to modify the SRLG TLV of type 138 to identify the link by IPv6 addresses, so a new TLV is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Four existing pieces of information name links and routers with IPv4 addresses: the router identifier, the local interface address, the neighbour's address and the shared risk groups. Each needs an IPv6 counterpart, and one of them, the shared risk group TLV, cannot simply be extended.

sections.title: The IPv6 Router ID and Address Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The IPv6 TE Router ID TLV is TLV type 140. It contains a 16-octet IPv6 address. A stable global IPv6 address must be used, so that the router ID provides a routable address regardless of the state of a node's interfaces. If a router does not implement traffic engineering it may include or omit the TLV. If a router implements traffic engineering for IPv6 it must include this TLV in its LSP, and it must not be included more than once in an LSP. An implementation receiving an IPv6 TE Router ID TLV must not consider the router ID as a /128 reachable prefix in the standard SPF calculation, because that can lead to forwarding loops when interacting with systems that do not support this TLV.

The IPv6 Interface Address sub-TLV of the Extended IS Reachability TLV has sub-TLV type 12. It contains a 16-octet IPv6 address for the interface described by the containing Extended IS Reachability TLV, and it can occur multiple times. Implementations must not inject a /128 prefix for the interface address into their routing or forwarding table, because that can lead to forwarding loops when interacting with systems that do not support this sub-TLV. If a router implements the basic TLV extensions of RFC 5305 it may include or omit this sub-TLV. If it implements IPv6 traffic engineering it must include it, except on an unnumbered point-to-point link, where the Link-Local Interface Identifiers sub-TLV is used instead. It must not contain an IPv6 link-local address.

The IPv6 Neighbor Address sub-TLV of the Extended IS Reachability TLV has sub-TLV type 13. It contains a 16-octet IPv6 address for a neighboring router on the link described by the main TLV, and it can occur multiple times. The same rule about not injecting a /128 prefix applies, and the same rules govern when it must be included: a router implementing IPv6 traffic engineering must include it for point-to-point links, except on an unnumbered point-to-point link where the Link-Local Interface Identifiers sub-TLV is used instead. It must not contain an IPv6 link-local address.
sections.plainLanguage: The router identifier names the router itself with a 16-byte address that does not change with its interfaces. The two sub-TLVs name the two ends of a link. None of them may carry a link-local address, and none of them may be turned into a host route, because an older router that does not know them would then black-hole traffic.

sections.title: The IPv6 SRLG TLV
sections.content:
The IPv6 SRLG TLV has type 139 and carries the Shared Risk Link Group information defined in RFC 4202. Its value is a data structure consisting of 6 octets of System ID, 1 octet of pseudonode number, 1 octet of flags, 16 octets of IPv6 interface address, an optional 16 octets of IPv6 neighbor address, and a variable list of SRLG values where each element in the list has 4 octets.

The neighbor is identified by its System ID of 6 octets plus one octet to indicate the pseudonode number if the neighbor is on a LAN interface. The 1-octet flags field has one flag defined: the NA bit, set to 1 when the IPv6 neighbor address is included and to 0 when it is not. Other bits in the flags field are reserved for future use. Any bit not understood by an implementation must be set to zero by the sender, and if a router receives an IPv6 SRLG TLV with non-zero values for any bit it does not understand, it must ignore the TLV, that is, not use it locally but flood it unchanged to its neighbours as normal. That rule is what allows alternative ways of identifying the link to be added later: an implementation that does not understand such an extension ignores the TLV rather than misinterpret it.

The length of the TLV is 24 plus 4 times the number of SRLG values, plus 16 if the IPv6 neighbor address is included.

To prevent an SRLG TLV and an IPv6 SRLG TLV in the same logical LSP from causing confusion, four rules apply. The IPv6 SRLG TLV may occur more than once within the IS-IS logical LSP. There must not be more than one IPv6 SRLG TLV for a given link. The IPv6 SRLG TLV of type 139 must not be used to describe the shared risk link groups for a given link if it is possible to use the SRLG TLV of type 138. If both an SRLG TLV and an IPv6 SRLG TLV are received describing the shared risk link groups for the same link, the receiver must apply the SRLG TLV and ignore the IPv6 SRLG TLV. In other words, if shared risk link groups are to be advertised for a link and the Extended IS Reachability TLV describing that link contains IPv4 interface or neighbor address sub-TLVs, or the link-local identifiers sub-TLV, then the groups must be advertised in the SRLG TLV of type 138.
sections.plainLanguage: The shared risk group TLV says which sets of links tend to fail together, so that a path can avoid depending on two links that share a fate. This one names the link with IPv6 addresses. It carries an optional neighbour address, and it can be extended later by adding flag bits, because a router that sees an unknown flag just passes the TLV on without using it.

sections.title: The IPv6 Global Interface Address TLV
sections.content:
The IPv6 Global Interface Address TLV is TLV type 233. Its structure is identical to that of the IPv6 Interface Address TLV defined in RFC 5308, but the semantics differ. The TLV is included in Hello PDUs for those interfaces that use the IPv6 traffic engineering extensions, and it contains the global or unique-local IPv6 addresses assigned to the interface that is sending the Hello. It is not used in LSPs.

This is the piece that makes the neighbour sub-TLV possible. A router next door needs a globally unique address for the far end of the link, and the IPv6 Interface Address TLV only carries link-local addresses in Hello PDUs, so a separate TLV is needed to carry the usable address.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbouring routers exchange Hello packets. This new field lets a router put its routable IPv6 address in that Hello, so the other end can name it in the shared risk group information it later advertises.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The document defines three new IS-IS TLV types, which IANA has reflected in the IS-IS TLV code point registry.

  • Type 139, IPv6 SRLG TLV, is carried in LSPs.
  • Type 140, IPv6 TE Router ID, is carried in LSPs.
  • Type 233, IPv6 Global Interface Address TLV, is carried in Hello PDUs.

It also defines two new sub-TLV types of top-level TLV 22, which IANA has reflected in the Sub-TLVs for TLV 22, 141 and 222 registry. Sub-TLV type 12 is the IPv6 Interface Address and sub-TLV type 13 is the IPv6 Neighbor Address. Both are valid in TLV 22, TLV 141 and TLV 222, and both are 16 octets long.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the list of IS-IS TLV numbers and where each one may appear. Three new numbers and two new sub-numbers are added here.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document raises no new security issues for IS-IS. For the general security considerations for IS-IS, see RFC 5304, IS-IS Cryptographic Authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new. The usual IS-IS authentication guidance applies, and these TLVs are covered by it in the same way as the existing ones.

fields.name: System ID
fields.desc: The system ID of the node the link belongs to.

fields.name: Pseudonode num
fields.desc: The pseudonode number, used when the neighbor is on a LAN interface.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: One flag is defined: NA, set to 1 when the IPv6 neighbor address is included. Other bits are reserved and must be set to zero if not understood.

fields.name: IPv6 interface address
fields.desc: The IPv6 address of the local end of the link.

fields.name: IPv6 neighbor address
fields.desc: Optional. The IPv6 address of the far end of the link, present when the NA flag is set.

fields.name: SRLG value
fields.desc: One shared risk link group value. The list is variable, with 4 octets per element.

viz.caption: The new IS-IS TLV and sub-TLV code points

items.label: IPv6 SRLG TLV
items.desc: Carried in LSPs. Names the link with IPv6 addresses and lists the shared risk link groups.

items.label: IPv6 TE Router ID
items.desc: Carried in LSPs. Holds a 16-octet IPv6 address identifying the traffic engineering node.

items.label: IPv6 Global Interface Address TLV
items.desc: Carried in Hello PDUs. Holds the global or unique-local addresses of the sending interface.

items.label: IPv6 Interface Address sub-TLV
items.desc: A sub-TLV of TLV 22, 141 and 222. Holds the 16-octet IPv6 address of the local end of a link.

items.label: IPv6 Neighbor Address sub-TLV
items.desc: A sub-TLV of TLV 22, 141 and 222. Holds the 16-octet IPv6 address of the far end of a link.
